The post Chiplet Co-Design Framework Reduces Energy and Design Costs for AI Accelerators (University of Michigan) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: The University of Michigan introduced 'Fengshui,' a co-design framework that optimizes chiplet pool composition alongside bespoke neural network accelerator design.
The framework targets the reduction of energy consumption and overall design costs, which are critical factors for scaling AI hardware.
By jointly optimizing the chiplet ecosystem and ASIC architecture, the tool provides a systematic approach to managing the complexity of modern heterogeneous AI accelerators.

The post Predicting Thermal Conductivity in Advanced BEOL Interconnect Stacks (Peking University) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Researchers at Peking University developed a structure-aware thermal conductivity modeling framework for BEOL interconnect stacks in advanced technology nodes.
The framework utilizes time-domain thermoreflectance measurements with 100 nm depth resolution to derive empirical relationships between interconnect structure and thermal conductivity.
By incorporating effective medium theory, the model enables predictive thermal analysis of spatial variations within 3D ICs, addressing a critical gap in current design tools.

The post Agentic AI Automates Design-Rule Repair While Preserving Layout Equivalence (Purdue University) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Purdue University researchers introduced 'DRC-Aid,' an agentic framework that automates the repair of design rule check (DRC) violations.
The system uses a deterministic rule engine to convert physical verification errors into a bounded set of geometric edits, constraining the search space for AI agents.
This approach aims to reduce manual design effort by automating local repairs while ensuring the final layout maintains strict equivalence to the original design.

The post AI in Chip Design: From Code Generation to EDA Orchestration (University of Edinburgh) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Researchers at the University of Edinburgh propose a shift in AI-driven EDA from simple code generation to hierarchical orchestration across design stages.
The study identifies a 'syntax trap' where current LLMs prioritize plausible code over physically correct hardware, leading to fragmented design context.
The paper advocates for standardized, physics-aware orchestrators that can coordinate decisions across the entire EDA flow to improve industrial scalability.

The post Reinforcement Learning Cuts Routing Violations in Dense Chip Layouts  (NYU) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: NYU researchers developed a history-aware offline reinforcement learning policy to address routing bottlenecks in high-density chip layouts.
The model predicts iterative cost weights for routers, improving convergence in dense regimes where traditional methods struggle to resolve persistent violations.
By leveraging existing router features, the approach enhances the physical design process without requiring significant changes to the underlying routing infrastructure.
